title: Which habits matter at every stage of a case interview?
description: You are being judged on how you come across in every minute, not just the answers. What to do, what to say, and the mistake to avoid.
hook: Some habits matter at every stage of a case: how you think aloud, how you handle a mistake, how you keep calm. Here they are in one place.
body:
Stage 10 of 10 in the ten stages of a case.

Why it matters

You are being judged on how you come across in every minute, not just the answers.

The common mistake

Letting nerves show, and losing the link to the goal.

What to do, and what to say

Presence

Keep smiling, especially when struggling. Pauses read as confidence. Treat it as a conversation between colleagues, not a test.

Good habits

Ask for time before taking it. Bring in personal experience and current events. If they mention capital spending, ask about running costs too.

Link everything back

Every answer, insight and calculation connects to the goal at the top of your page. Interviewers often mention it in feedback.

"...and this matters because our client’s goal is X."

Practise the moment

Read the situation and say your answer out loud before you open the model.

You’ve just given an answer about falling sales in one region. Add a habit that separates strong candidates.

Show a strong answer

"...and this matters because our client’s goal is to get back to $10M profit within two years."

Why it works: Linking back to the goal is one of the habits interviewers mention most in feedback.

The interviewer mentions the new plant will cost $150M to build. What do you ask about?

Show a strong answer

"And what would it cost to run each year?" (When you hear capital spending, ask about running costs.)

Why it works: Investment cases are decided on both the upfront and the ongoing cost.

Keep facts, hypotheses and decisions distinct

During a case you might know that a store's footfall fell 15%, suspect that a new competitor caused it, and tentatively recommend a loyalty offer. Those are three different kinds of statements. Label them accurately: fact, hypothesis, proposed test or action.

Clear labelling prevents a common mistake: treating an attractive early explanation as proven evidence. It also makes it easy to revise the structure when new information arrives. A candidate who changes their mind after seeing contrary data is demonstrating judgement, not weakness.
